meta.title: "Perfect or not at all" — and your child never even starts? | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to see the process instead of the extremes and allow themselves to do it "well enough", not "perfectly". Game-based critical thinking course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: Does your child refuse to start because "it won't be perfect anyway"?
hero.subheadline: "If it's not the best, then why bother." "Either I do it brilliantly or not at all." The bar shoots straight to maximum — and the action stops before it even begins. Easier not to try than to do it "imperfectly".

media.alt: A child not starting something out of fear of doing it imperfectly

pain.title: It's not a high standard — it's the "perfect or failure" trap
pain.body:
The child (often themselves) leaves only two options: either it comes out perfect, or it's a failure. As if there's no third. But between those extremes lies the whole process — the first uncertain attempts, the mistakes, the small steps that a result actually grows from.

This isn't laziness or indifference. The child is caught in a rigid frame where "imperfect" equals "bad". Without the skill to see the process, they choose not to do it at all — to avoid the feeling of not being "good enough".

The result — the child doesn't even give themselves a chance to try. They don't start drawing, writing, or performing, because they're afraid it won't be perfect — and so they never find out that they could.

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 40 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Notices the "perfect or not at all" moment
🧠 Sees the process — the tries and mistakes — between the extremes
💬 Understands: imperfect isn't failure, it's a step
🛡️ Lets themselves start and do it "well enough" instead of waiting for perfect

social_proof.quote: My daughter used to tear up a drawing if it came out "not right". Now she says "this is only the first try" — and just keeps going. Getting started became easier than freezing in front of perfect.
social_proof.author: Svitlana, mum of 9-year-old Eva

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 8–12 year olds. At this age, children are most receptive to new thinking patterns and haven't yet formed rigid biases.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
